prompt: According to the passage, pools A and B differed from pools C and D in that
passage:
Every March the pale salamanders of the Radna hills leave the limestone crevices where they have wintered and travel, some of them two hundred meters, to breed in shallow rock pools. For most of the last century the standard account held that each animal remembered its route. Teodora Vasnev, a field biologist who had spent eleven winters in the hills, thought the account did no work. Memory, she liked to say, was the name of the puzzle and not its solution.

In 1996 she built something that let her ask a narrower question. Four artificial pools, identical basins of poured concrete, were sunk into a level clearing forty meters from any natural water, at the corners of a square eight meters on a side. She labeled them A through D. Under pools A and B she set a small motor that tapped the basin twice a second, the rate of water dripping from stone; under pools C and D she set motors that never ran. Nothing else about the four differed: the same water, the same depth, the same rim of gravel. At dusk she carried ninety-six adults from three home crevices to the center of the square and left them there.

Averaged over eleven nights across two springs, sixty-one of the ninety-six were in A or B by dawn, twenty-two were still in the open, and thirteen were in C or D. The pattern held on nine nights of the eleven.

The untreated pools were the informative ones. Pool D took no animal at all until, on the last three nights, she shifted it three meters east toward the release point; it then took thirty a night, more than either tapping pool. Vasnev put this in the body of the paper rather than in a footnote.

In the second season she drew the path of every animal on a sheet of waxed paper laid over a map of the clearing, to learn whether the animals approached the pools directly or by searching. The lines ran straight from the release point and bent only in the last two meters.

She published in 1999, in a journal few outside the region read, and for a decade the work was cited mainly by people who studied cave fish. What makes it worth reading now is less the cue she found than the way she isolated it: she built a clearing in which only one question could be asked at a time, and then reported the one result that spoiled the answer.

a liter of the animals' own breeding water was stirred in
their water was held two degrees warmer than the ground
dark boards above them kept the water in shade
correct_answer: a motor beneath them tapped the basins twice a second
explanation: The apparatus paragraph specifies "a small motor that tapped the basin twice a second, the rate of water dripping from stone."

prompt: According to the passage, the works the commission adopted in December 1893 consisted of
passage:
Port Alden sits at the mouth of a shallow bay, on a coast the Admiralty charts of the period marked simply as sand, shifting. A current runs along that coast from the west, carrying sand eastward past the town all winter. For most of the nineteenth century the fishing fleet lay at anchor in the open, and in a hard gale the boats were hauled up the beach by hand. In 1893, after two winters in which nine boats were lost, the borough appointed a harbour commission and gave it a single instruction: make the inner basin safe. The commission's engineer was Marguerite Hallam, then thirty-four, who had built two river locks and no sea works at all.

Hallam laid four schemes before the commissioners that autumn, and in December they adopted a stone mole, six hundred yards long, run out from the eastern headland to shelter the basin behind it. Work began in the spring of 1894 and was finished, at a cost of eleven thousand pounds, in the autumn of 1897. For three seasons it seemed to answer. Insurance rates for the Port Alden boats fell by a fifth, and the borough borrowed against the improvement to pave the fish quay.

The county inspection of 1901 ended that confidence. The surveyors found that the mole had done what any wall set across a sand-bearing current will do: the anchorage behind it had silted to four feet at low water, and the deepest berths were gone. From 1902 skippers who had wintered at Port Alden for thirty years began running instead for the deeper harbour at Wexham, eleven miles east, and landing their catch there. Port Alden's winter earnings fell by rather more than a third within four years, and the quay loan, secured on a trade that had moved away, was not cleared until 1926.

Hallam's method was, in the strict sense, conservative: she had done what the profession then held to be safe, and she had done it well. Her defence, when it came, rested on the two soundings of the bay that existed in 1893, one of them thirty years old, neither of them extending east of the headland. Hallam left the coast in 1903 and never took sea work again.

a stone mole six hundred yards long run out from the eastern headland
a dredged approach channel twelve feet deep cut through the bar, and no barrier
a pair of ninety-yard timber jetties narrowing the mouth of the inner basin
correct_answer: a stone mole six hundred yards long run out from the eastern headland
explanation: The commissioners "adopted a stone mole, six hundred yards long, run out from the eastern headland to shelter the basin behind it."

prompt: According to the passage, what did Solberg and Whitfield change about the stand in the third summer?
passage:
For six summers, Ivar Solberg and Dana Whitfield studied a single unattended vegetable stand on a county road in northern Vermont. The stand belonged to the Trask family, who set out crates of produce each morning, posted a price list, and left a locked steel box for payment. No one watched the road. Solberg and Whitfield wanted to know what people do when the only thing holding up a price is the price itself.

Their method was deliberately dull. Each evening an assistant weighed what remained, counted the money, and computed a compliance rate: money received divided by money owed. Across the first two summers that rate sat between 61 and 64 percent and barely moved from one day of the week to the next. Two customers in five paid nothing at all; a much smaller group paid above the list price, apparently covering for the rest.

In the third summer the researchers changed one thing. They mounted a small mirror on the post above the cash box, angled so that anyone reaching for the slot met their own face for a moment. Whitfield's reasoning was that people behave differently when reminded of being watched, even when the watcher is themselves.

The season that followed is the part of the study people cite. Compliance in the hours before noon, when the mirror caught the light, averaged 81 percent; in the shaded afternoon it averaged 62 percent. The two figures were reported side by side rather than folded into a season average, and the gap between them is the finding.

Solberg is cautious about what a number like that can carry. The stand sits on one road in one county, and the drivers who stop there are not a random sample of anyone; a stand outside a city, he notes, might behave nothing like it. The result registered with the Trask family long before it reached any table of his; they had been saying for years that mornings paid better than afternoons, and Solberg allows that the study mostly caught up with what the people running the stand already knew.
choices: They mounted a small mirror above the cash box, angled toward anyone reaching for the slot.
They cut every price by a third and rounded it so no purchase required change.
They posted, beside each price, the share of customers who had paid in full the week before.
They replaced the steel box with a clear one that showed the bills already inside.
correct_answer: They mounted a small mirror above the cash box, angled toward anyone reaching for the slot.
explanation: The passage says they "mounted a small mirror on the post above the cash box, angled so that anyone reaching for the slot met their own face."

prompt: During her first four months in Serrano's shop, what work was the narrator given?
passage:
The shop smelled of felt and hot glue, and I have not walked past an open piano since without checking, out of habit, whether the lid is propped at the angle Serrano preferred. I was fifteen when my mother left me at his door with a note saying only that I was willing. He read it twice, folded it into his apron pocket, and then did not speak to me about tuning for a long while.

For the first four months he sat me on a stool beneath the raised lid of whatever instrument he was working on, and had me count. Two strings of a unison, struck together, throb at a rate; I was to say the number of throbs in a second, aloud, and be corrected until I was right. I was not permitted to put a tool to a string.

I had come expecting hammers and wire. I had a picture of myself in it, too: the small tool, the held breath, the string coming true under my hand. Devlin, the other apprentice, who had arrived a season ahead of me, told me not to ask what any of it was for. I asked anyway, in February, when my patience gave out.

He said that a tuner is a witness before he is a workman, and that most of the damage done in the trade is done by men whose hands are quicker than their ears. "A doctor who cannot hear a heart," he said, "may still own a very fine stethoscope." What I had once heard, he said, I could not afterward pretend not to have heard.

Then he turned back to the instrument on the bench and left me to make of it what I could. I did not understand him that winter. I understood him, I think, on a Tuesday four years later, in a rented hall in Trentham, when a piano I had been given two hours to prepare went wrong under my hands and I found that I already knew what to do without deciding to know it.

Serrano died the spring before last. I have his bench now, and three apprentices of my own, and every one of them asks me in February the question I asked him.

What he gave me was not a technique but a way of waiting, and I have had to be careful since not to make a virtue of the waiting itself. I tell my three the truth: the counting is dull, and a season of it will cost them nothing they will miss. Then I put them under the lid and leave them there. Close listening is the whole of the trade; the lever only carries out what the ear has already settled.
choices: Playing scales and easy pieces badly for an hour a day with the door open.
Counting aloud the throbs between two struck strings from a stool beneath the raised lid.
Filing chisels at the vise and cutting the shop's whole set of wedge mutes by hand.
Carrying the cases and writing in a ledger what each customer's room and habits were.
correct_answer: Counting aloud the throbs between two struck strings from a stool beneath the raised lid.
explanation: The passage states he "sat me on a stool beneath the raised lid... and had me count," saying "the number of throbs in a second, aloud."

prompt: Osei's four seasons of counting hollows showed that abandonment tracked which of the following?
passage:
On the gravel flats of the Karoo, the mottled nightjar builds nothing at all. The female scrapes a shallow hollow in the open ground, lays two eggs the colour of lichen, and settles over them so still that a hiker can pass within a metre and never look down. The arrangement works: in four seasons of watching, fewer than one nest in ten was found by a fox or a crow. Which is what makes the birds' other habit so hard to explain. In roughly a third of nests the pair simply walks away. The eggs are intact; the two birds scrape a fresh hollow somewhere else and begin again.

Mira Osei spent those four seasons near Loxton, on her knees with a notebook, counting hollows. The departures were not scattered evenly. They tracked the temperature of the ground: days when the flats passed fifty degrees at midday were followed, four times in five, by an abandonment, while a cool week produced almost none. The pattern held in early nests and late ones alike.

The obvious suspect was predation — a fox passing close enough to unsettle a pair without ever finding the clutch. Osei tested the idea by moving eggs between hollows. Eggs carried to a hollow in the morning shade of the dolerite ridge were sat through the hottest week of December, whatever pair had laid them. The same eggs' parents, left out on the open flats, walked off within three days. The trigger travelled with the ground's heat, not with the clutch or with the birds.

The pairs that left did not stay low; the new hollow lay on average nine hundred metres uphill, on the dolerite ridge where rock holds the morning cool. Osei read ground temperatures at both. The open flats reached fifty-four degrees by one o'clock; the ridge hollows stayed near thirty. By January the heat had put a check on laying everywhere below the rock, and every hollow still occupied lay above it.

None of this makes the nightjar a planner. The bird holds no model of the season in its head; it holds a rule, and the rule was shaped by what the flats did to birds that lacked it. What the case offers is a reminder that behaviour which looks like waste from the outside may be the cheapest line in the animal's budget — and that the way to find out is to count, for four seasons, the things nobody thought worth counting.
choices: the temperature of the open ground at midday
the number of days the hollow had been in use
the position of the hollow relative to the channels
the recent size of the moth traps' catch
correct_answer: the temperature of the open ground at midday
explanation: The departures "tracked the temperature of the ground: days when the flats passed fifty degrees at midday were followed, four times in five, by an abandonment."
